q: You are putting the genoa sheet on this winch. Which way do the turns go round the drum?
a: Clockwise
o: Anticlockwise
Clockwise to port, anticlockwise to starboard
Either way: the drum turns both ways
why: Yacht winches turn clockwise only, so the sheet goes on clockwise.

q: You have finished winding in the genoa sheet. What do you do with the winch handle?
a: Take it out and put it in its pocket
o: Leave it in the winch for next time
Leave it in, turned to point aft
Lay it on the cockpit seat nearby
why: A handle left in the winch fouls sheets and people, and is easily knocked overboard.

q: You have motored out of the harbour and the sails are going up. What do you do with the fenders?
a: Take them in and stow them
o: Leave them out for the next harbour
Lower them to touch the water
Tie them up higher on the guardrail
why: Fenders hanging at sea bang the hull and get lost; bring them in once clear of the harbour.

q: Coming alongside, you stand by with the bow line coiled. When do you get off onto the pontoon?
a: When the boat is close and nearly stopped, by stepping
o: As soon as you can jump the gap
When the bow first touches the pontoon
Before the boat slows, to save time
why: Step, never jump: a jump can end between the boat and the pontoon.

q: A crew member is winding the winch and you are tailing. What is your job?
a: Keep steady tension on the tail as it comes off
o: Hold the tail loosely so it can slip
Push the turns down the drum with your hand
Let go of the tail whenever they pause
why: Without tension on the tail the sheet slips on the drum and the winding is wasted.

q: This winch is a self-tailer. How do you load the sheet so you can wind with both hands?
a: A few turns clockwise, then into the jaws on top
o: One turn anticlockwise, then into the jaws
Straight into the jaws with no turns
Turns clockwise, then cleat the tail below
why: The turns grip the drum; the jaws on top hold the tail, so no one needs to tail.

q: Winding in the genoa sheet, you see this, and the sheet will neither come in nor ease. What do you do?
a: Stop, keep your hands clear and call the skipper
o: Keep winding: it will free itself
Pull the crossed turns off by hand
Take the handle out and spin the drum back
why: A riding turn locks a loaded sheet; fingers near the drum can be trapped.

q: The skipper asks you to ease the loaded genoa sheet a little. How do you do it?
a: Ease the tail out slowly, fingers clear of the turns
o: Take all the turns off and hold the tail
Wind the winch handle backwards
Wrap the tail once round your hand for grip
why: A loaded sheet can jerk, and fingers near the drum get pulled into the turns.

q: You are getting the fenders ready for tonight's berth. Where do you hang them?
a: Both sides, at the widest part, level with the neighbours
o: At the stern only, hanging low down by the water
At the bow only, to protect the anchor and pulpit
One side only, the side the wind is coming from
why: Stern-to, your sides lie against the yachts next to you, so the fenders go on both sides.

fig.title: Stern-to tonight
lines: Yachts already berthed on both sides
Quay about 1 m above the water

q: The skipper points at your fenders as you come in. What do you change?
a: Lower them to where the pontoon will touch the hull
o: Nothing: at deck level they guard the rail
Raise them higher, to the top of the rail
Take them in: a pontoon is soft
why: Fenders hang where the hull meets the pontoon edge, here close to the water.

fig.title: Coming alongside
lines: Your fenders hang at deck level

q: Alongside, the skipper asks you to rig a spring from the bow cleat. Where does it lead ashore?
a: Aft along the quay, to a bollard near the stern
o: Straight across, to the nearest bollard
Forward along the quay, ahead of the bow
Back to the boat's own stern cleat
why: A spring runs diagonally: from the bow it leads aft, from the stern it leads forward.

q: Med mooring, you have walked the lazy line up to the bow cleat. What do you do before making it fast?
a: Haul it in hard until it is taut, then cleat it
o: Leave some slack so the boat can swing
Pass it back to the marinero to hold
Cleat it slack: it is only a back-up
why: The lazy line does the anchor's job: pulled taut, it holds the bow off and the stern clear of the quay.

q: You are at the stern as the boat backs in. What do you do?
a: Put a loose fender in the gap and keep your hands out
o: Push the boat off the quay with your foot
Hold the stern off with both hands
Jump onto the quay and push the boat off
why: Never put hands or feet between boat and quay: tonnes of boat will crush them.

fig.title: Stern-to, the last metre
lines: The stern swings towards the quay corner
No fender hangs at that spot
You are standing at the stern

q: The tender is towed astern on a long painter, and the skipper is about to reverse into a berth. What do you do with the painter?
a: Shorten it or bring the tender alongside, clear of the prop
o: Let it out longer so the tender trails clear
Leave it: going astern, the tender drifts away
Hand it to the helm to hold while reversing
why: Going astern the boat runs over a slack painter, and it can wrap round the propeller.

q: Before leaving, the skipper asks you to rig the stern line as a slip line, so you can let it go from on board. What do you do?
a: Lead it round the bollard and back, both ends cleated aboard
o: Tie a second line to the same bollard as a back-up
Make it fast with two cleat hitches on the boat's cleat
Tie a bowline round the bollard instead of a hitch
why: With both ends aboard, you let one end go and pull the line back round the bollard.

q: The tender is alongside and the crew are climbing down into it. When do you untie the painter?
a: Last, when everyone is in and seated
o: First, so it is ready to go
When the first person is in
Before boarding, then hold it by hand
why: While the painter is tied on, the tender cannot drift off as people climb in.

q: You are helping the skipper clear a riding turn. What is the next step?
a: Winch in the spare line, then clear the slack turns
o: Cut the jammed sheet, as it is backed up
Wind the jammed winch harder to free it
Untie the spare line now it has gripped
why: The spare line takes the load; only an unloaded sheet can be unwound safely.

fig.title: Riding turn
lines: Genoa sheet jammed on the winch
Spare line tied on with a rolling hitch
Spare line led to the other winch

q: The wind pushes the boat along the quay. Which lines take the strain?
a: The stern line and the spring led aft from the bow
o: The bow line and the spring led forward from the stern
Only the bow line, as the boat moves forward
All four lines share the load equally
why: Lines leading aft from the boat stop it moving forward: the stern line and the spring from the bow.

fig.title: Alongside, starboard side-to
lines: The boat is pushed forward along the quay
Lines: bow, stern and two springs

q: Coming alongside, you are to step ashore with a line. Where on deck do you step off from?
a: By the shrouds, where the boat is widest and closest
o: Right at the bow, as it arrives first
From the bathing platform at the stern
From the coachroof, for extra height
why: At the shrouds the boat is widest and steadiest, and there is something to hold as you step.

q: Which stern line do you pass ashore first?
a: The port one, on the windward side
o: The starboard one, on the leeward side
Both together, one in each hand
Whichever is nearer the marinero
why: The windward line stops the stern blowing downwind onto the neighbours.

fig.title: Reversing stern-to
lines: Two stern lines ready, one each side
